fall resulting in fatal injury

delayed CT head

administration of enoxaparin

inadequate record keeping

omission of enoxaparin use in reports



A series of miscommunications between; nursing staff, junior and consultant paediatric medical staff resulted in concerns regarding Aman not being properly considered prior to discharge. Staff relied on assumptions that others understood the factors affecting Aman and had a plan to resolve them, this was not the case. Had effective communication occurred it was unlikely that Aman would have been discharged.
miscommunication among nursing staff, junior and consultant paediatric medical staff


The doctor who authorised discharge did not satisfy himself of the most recent set of clinical observations and associated Paediatric Early Warning Sign (PEWS) score prior to discharge.
failure to verify recent clinical observations and PEWS score before discharge



The Paediatric Emergency Department was particularly busy that evening, with a combination of high patient numbers and severe acuity of symptoms. The accounts provided by Trust witnesses was that resulted in a pressurised environment and that this was a situation that occurred with an increasing level of frequency over the last two years.
operational pressure in paediatric emergency department



Following admission, Mrs Toye was not assessed for risks of malnutrition by use of the MUST score system. Such an assessment was required for all patients. Erroneously, her notes recorded that she scored Oon the MUST scale which meant that no other staff members began an assessment throughout her admission. It is likely that during admission Mrs Toye would have scored 4 on a MUST assessment, as such a number of mitigations would have been introduced to maximise her nutritional intake.
lack of nutrition assessment


Contemporary audits of compliance of Must scoring on the ward in question demonstrate that one in ten patients are not being assessed for risks of malnutrition.
inadequate nutrition risk assessment compliance


Instructions on the management of the NG tube were provided on a ward round by a consultant, the instructions were not clearly noted by the House Officer accompanying the consultant.
inadequate documentation of NG tube management instructions


Nursing staff had no clinical instruction as to how to manage the NG tube.
absence of clinical instruction for NG tube management


Nursing staff dealing with the patient were agency staff without training or experience of NG tube management.
inexperienced agency staff managing NG tube


Concerns regarding the NG tube function were not properly escalated to clinical staff.
failure to escalate NG tube concerns

lack of renal monitoring

failure to classify serious incident


Mr O'Neill was known to be a restless patient during a dialysis session. This factor must have increased the risk of needle dislodgement.
needle dislodgement during dialysis


Mr O'Neill was a frail patient with little reserve and would be more likely to swiftly lose consciousness following a bleed.
rapid loss of consciousness after bleed


Mr O'Neill was placed in a position which was outside of a clear line of sight from the nurses station.
patient out of nurses' line of sight

insufficient alarm sensitivity for bleed detection
